def: Describes the stage of ovarian follicle development before an antrum (fluid-filled cavity) forms, including primordial, primary and secondary follicles.
The first stage of change in the transtheoretical model, in which a person is not yet thinking about changing a behavior such as smoking.
Occurring before the liver. Prehepatic jaundice comes from excess bilirubin production, as in hemolysis, and gives unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Before a girl's first menstrual period (menarche).

An intermediate-size trinucleotide repeat expansion that does not cause full disease but can expand in the next generation. FMR1 premutation causes fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome and primary ovarian insufficiency.
Breathing high-concentration oxygen before anesthesia induction or intubation to fill the lungs with oxygen and extend safe time without breathing.
Describes the lightheaded, faint feeling before fainting, with dim vision and weakness, without total loss of consciousness.
In front of the trachea. The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid, and pretracheal nodes drain the thyroid and larynx.
The earliest cluster of cells in the embryo that develops into an organ or structure, such as the lung bud or the thyroid primordium.
Describes pristanic acid, a branched-chain fatty acid derived from phytanic acid that is broken down in peroxisomes. It accumulates in peroxisomal disorders such as Refsum disease.
Tending to cause or worsen abnormal heart rhythms. Many antiarrhythmic drugs, such as class IC agents and those that prolong the QT interval, can be proarrhythmic.
The inactive precursor of carboxypeptidase, secreted by the pancreas and activated in the intestine by trypsin.
Chemicals that are not cancer-causing until the body, often cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver, converts them into active carcinogens. Aflatoxin B1 is an example.
The ability of an enzyme, such as DNA polymerase, to add many nucleotides in a row before detaching from the template. A sliding clamp increases it.
Complete prolapse of an organ outside the body, most often the uterus protruding through the vaginal opening.
Pain in the rectum or anal area. Proctalgia fugax is sudden, brief rectal pain from muscle spasm.
The inactive precursor of elastase, an enzyme secreted by the pancreas and activated in the intestine by trypsin.
The segments of an adult tapeworm that contain reproductive organs and eggs. They detach and pass in stool, as in Taenia and Diphyllobothrium.
Presence of prolactin in the blood, usually meaning hyperprolactinemia, which causes galactorrhea, amenorrhea and low libido. Causes include prolactinoma, pregnancy and dopamine antagonist drugs.
A reaction that looks like allergy but is not triggered by IgE antibodies. Drugs such as opioids, vancomycin and contrast media can directly activate mast cells.
Right lower abdominal pain that mimics appendicitis but has another cause, such as mesenteric adenitis from Yersinia infection.
False outpouchings of the gut wall lacking all layers; only mucosa and submucosa herniate. Colonic diverticula and Zenker diverticulum are examples.
Narrow bands of bone lucency perpendicular to the cortex, called Looser zones, seen in osteomalacia and rickets from vitamin D deficiency.
Apparent breast enlargement in men caused by fat deposition rather than true glandular tissue growth, common in obesity.
An exudate of fibrin, dead cells and bacteria that forms a false membrane on a mucosal surface. It is seen in Clostridioides difficile colitis and diphtheria.
Exudates of fibrin, dead cells and bacteria forming false membranes on mucosa, as in C. difficile colitis and diphtheria.
Describes a growth pattern of cells around fibrovascular cores that looks like papillae but is formed by degeneration. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm is a tumor of the pancreas in young women.
A raised island of regenerating or inflamed mucosa, surrounded by ulcers, that resembles a polyp. It is seen in long-standing inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.
Raised islands of regenerating or inflamed colon mucosa surrounded by ulcers, resembling polyps. They occur in inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.
Tumor cells arranged around a central blood vessel rather than around a true lumen. They are classic in ependymoma and also seen in medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma.
An episode that looks like an epileptic seizure but lacks abnormal brain electrical activity, usually of psychogenic origin (functional seizure).
An apparent faint with no true loss of cerebral blood flow, though the person seems unresponsive. It is usually psychogenic.
The part of the levator ani that forms a sling around the anorectal junction. It maintains fecal continence by angling the rectum forward.
Surgery that reconstructs the renal pelvis and ureteropelvic junction to relieve a blockage and hydronephrosis.
Describes a nucleus that has shrunk, condensed and stained very dark, an irreversible sign of cell death (pyknosis), followed by karyorrhexis and karyolysis.
Surgery that widens the pylorus, the outlet of the stomach, to improve gastric emptying, as in vagotomy or gastroparesis.
A bacterial enzyme that converts pyrazinamide into its active form pyrazinoic acid. Loss of this enzyme causes pyrazinamide resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Describes pyrazinoic acid, the active form of pyrazinamide produced inside Mycobacterium tuberculosis by pyrazinamidase. It disrupts the membrane and energy of the bacillus.
Relating to the radius and the carpal bones. The radiocarpal joint is the wrist joint between the radius and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum.
Areas that block X-rays and appear white on radiographs, such as bone, metal and calcifications.
Blocking X-rays and appearing white on radiographs, as bone, metal and some stones do.
A phase of toddler development (about 15-24 months) in which the child alternates between exploring independently and returning to the caregiver for reassurance.
The reforming of double-stranded DNA from separated single strands upon cooling. The speed of reannealing is used to study DNA complexity and repeats.
Reopening of a blocked blood vessel, as the lumen reforms after a clot or after treatment such as thrombolysis.
Bending light so that it looks bright or shiny under the microscope. Refractile crystals or bodies, such as calcium oxalate, stand out in polarized light.
